name: Hair oiling

card.summary: Applying oil to hair and scalp, a long-standing South Asian practice; lab data and surveys exist, but growth or anti-graying claims lack trials.
card.note: Evidence is limited to lab fiber tests, a case-control study and self-reported surveys; scalp irritation and dandruff are reported by some users.

quick.overview:
Hair oiling is the practice of applying oils such as coconut oil to the hair and scalp, often with a massage and often left on for some hours. It is deeply rooted in Indian culture and has been spread further by social media.

The research is thin. A laboratory study found that coconut oil, but not mineral oil, changed the mechanical properties of hair fibers after repeated washes. A case-control study found that oiling appeared protective against premature graying, and a large Indian survey recorded dandruff, itch and hair fall among participants.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say oils condition the hair and nourish the scalp. In lab tests of single hair fibers, penetration of coconut oil was reported to make the fiber core more flexible, helping it cope with twisting stress. No trial has shown that oiling increases hair growth.
quick.risks: In a 2026 survey of 1,200 people in southern India, 25 percent reported dandruff, 15 percent an itchy scalp and 10 percent hair fall, and many with scalp problems said they would consider changing their routine on dermatologist advice. The survey is self-reported and cannot show cause.

lead: Hair oiling is the application of oils, often coconut oil or herbal blends, to the hair and scalp, usually with a massage. It is a traditional practice in India, where a head massage called champi is common and often uses oil or herbal preparations. [1][2]

Research is limited. Laboratory work has tested how oils affect hair fibers, a case-control study found an association between hair oiling and lower odds of premature graying, and a large survey in southern India described the prevalence of dandruff, itch and hair fall among people who oil. [3][4][5] The practice has also become a topic of debate among dermatologists, who weigh possible benefits and risks. [5]

paras: Champi is a traditional Indian head massage usually done with hair oil, and the English word shampoo derives from it. In India the practice remains common, using oils or herbal preparations such as neem, amla, fenugreek and almond. [1] The 2026 survey describes hair oiling as deeply rooted in Indian culture and long popular despite the rise of modern hair-care products and social media influence. [5]

A 2021 laboratory study tested coconut oil and mineral oil on hair swatches using single-fiber tensile and torsional tests. After a single wash there was no significant difference in most parameters, but after 20 wash cycles differences emerged, and when hair was twisted and extended, coconut oil differed from mineral oil even after one cycle. The authors attributed this to coconut oil penetrating the fiber and making the core more flexible. [3]

No randomized trials of hair oiling for hair growth or scalp health were found. A 2018 case-control study in North India of 120 patients with premature graying and 120 controls found that hair oiling seemed to protect against premature graying, alongside associations with family history, smoking, stress and lower serum ferritin, calcium and vitamin B12. [4]

A 2026 online survey of 1,200 participants in southern India found dandruff in 25 percent, itchy scalp in 15 percent and hair fall in 10 percent; 60 percent of those with scalp issues said they would consider changing their oiling practice on dermatological advice. The authors acknowledge reliance on self-reporting and regional bias. [5]

The survey authors describe dandruff, itch and hair fall as scalp issues reported among people who oil, and note that dermatologists debate the potential benefits and risks. [5] The survey design does not establish that oiling caused these problems.

timeline.event: Dean Mahomed opens baths in Brighton offering champi as therapeutic massage. [1]
